title: The nuclear club
hook: Nine countries have nuclear weapons. Four others once had them and gave them up.
notes: Warhead numbers are estimates by the Federation of American Scientists (Status of World Nuclear Forces 2025); governments do not publish exact figures. They count all warheads in each country's inventory, including retired ones awaiting dismantlement. First test dates are widely documented. Israel neither confirms nor denies having nuclear weapons. Nuclear sharing arrangements are reported, not officially itemised.

scenes.title: Joining the club
scenes.text: The United States tested the first nuclear bomb in 1945. The Soviet Union followed in 1949, then Britain, France and China. India, Pakistan and North Korea came later. Israel is widely believed to have weapons but has never said so. Press Play.

scenes.title: How many weapons
scenes.text: Russia and the United States hold almost nine in ten of the world's roughly 12,200 nuclear warheads: about 5,500 and 5,200. China's arsenal, around 600, is the fastest-growing. Britain, France, India, Pakistan, Israel and North Korea each have a few hundred or fewer. All of these numbers are estimates.

scenes.title: Fewer than at the peak
scenes.text: At the height of the Cold War, in 1986, the world had about 70,000 warheads. Arms-control treaties and dismantlement cut that by more than four-fifths. But the decline has stalled, and several countries are now adding weapons again.

scenes.title: The ones who gave them up
scenes.text: South Africa built six bombs in secret and dismantled them before ending apartheid. When the Soviet Union broke up, Ukraine, Belarus and Kazakhstan found themselves with nuclear weapons on their soil; all were sent to Russia by 1996.

scenes.title: Weapons on other countries' soil
scenes.text: Some countries host weapons that belong to others. Under NATO arrangements, US bombs are reported to be stored in Belgium, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands and Turkey. In 2023 Russia announced it had placed weapons in Belarus.
